title: Split a command line
description:
A process receives its command line as one string and splits it into arguments. Write `splitCommandLine(line)` using these rules (a simplified version of what Windows programs do):

- Arguments are separated by one or more spaces.
- A double quote `"` starts or ends a quoted section. Spaces inside a quoted section are part of the argument. The quote characters themselves are not part of it.
- Quoted and unquoted parts next to each other belong to the same argument: `--name="Rook Smith"` is the single argument `--name=Rook Smith`.
- `""` on its own is an empty argument.
- Leading and trailing spaces produce no arguments.

```
editor.exe --level "forest 2"     ->  { "editor.exe", "--level", "forest 2" }
"C:\My Games\a.exe" -x            ->  { "C:\My Games\a.exe", "-x" }
a "" b                            ->  { "a", "", "b" }
```
hints: Walk through the characters keeping three things: the argument being built, whether you are inside quotes, and whether an argument has started (needed so that `""` still counts as an argument).
A quote toggles "inside quotes" and marks the argument as started. A space outside quotes ends the current argument, if one has started. Anything else is added to the argument.
After the loop, push the last argument if one was started.
